query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, aluminide-based surface coating to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale during high‐temperature exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a thin aluminide-based coating on the alloy surface (via methods such as pack cementation or sputtering).
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation conditions in air at approximately 800 °C for a duration of 5 hours, with operational loading conditions corresponding to strain rates of 10^(–4)–10^(–2) s^(–1).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy’s surface as a result of the aluminide coating reacting with ambient oxygen.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide coating preferentially oxidizes to form an adherent, slow-growing alumina layer that acts as a diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress, thereby mitigating deleterious internal oxidation without altering the bulk properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the coated alloy will exhibit a significantly reduced oxide scale thickness and weight gain, with preservation of its room- and high-temperature mechanical performance following 5 hours of air exposure at 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr experiences substantial oxidation (leading to ‘pesting’) under similar conditions, degrading its mechanical integrity.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable for exposures around 800 °C in atmospheric air for up to 5 hours and under mechanical loading conditions typical of previous tensile tests (strain rates of 10^(–4)–10^(–2) s^(–1)), while striving to maintain the alloy’s ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness and process parameters that ensure formation of a consistent alumina scale without compromising ductility remain to be fully determined, as does the long-term stability of the coating under cyclic thermal-mechanical loading.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one with the aluminide coating applied and one untreated control group. Expose both groups to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS) to assess oxide scale formation and conduct tensile tests to evaluate any changes in ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (using SEM/EDS)
Post-exposure tensile ductility and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar or increased oxide scale thickness or weight gain) or if their tensile ductility and yield strength degrade compared to the untreated controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
